task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of July 15, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style reported feature about the crew sorting waste after the Grey Orchard fair and the practical work behind organizers' reuse and recycling claims.

facts.text: A cleanup note dated Monday, July 13, 2026, records Cairn Sorting Services checking material collected after the July 10-12 Grey Orchard fair.
The contractor assigned eight paid workers to the post-event collection and sorting operation.
The recorded material totaled 7.2 metric tons: four sent as residual waste, 1.8 accepted for recycling and 1.4 accepted for composting.
Material accepted by a processor is not a measured final output of recycled products or finished compost.
Some packaging labeled biodegradable was outside the receiving composter's accepted-material list.
The contractor used that specific processor's rules rather than assuming every package with an environmental label belonged in the same stream.
Food residue and mixed materials required workers to separate items that attendees had placed together.
Crew leader Omi Farden says vendor purchasing decisions affect the sorting work before visitors reach a bin.
Farden said, "The person choosing the cup and the person emptying the bin are making parts of the same decision."
The fair issued 4,000 reusable cups under a $2 return-deposit scheme and recorded 3,800 returned, a 95% return rate.
The 200 unreturned cups are not all proven discarded; some may have been kept, and their later destinations were not tracked.
Returned cups still required washing, transport and storage before another event could use them.
Food vendor Ceri Hollen says switching packaging is difficult when approved suppliers sell only in large minimum quantities.
Hollen said, "I can buy the right container and still be left with a year's supply after one weekend."
The organizer's waste contract has a fixed service fee plus actual processor charges, so lower residual weight does not remove every cleanup cost.
The reporting record contains no complete comparison with the previous fair's product mix, attendance or waste arrangements.
The fair recorded 12,000 entries over three days, including people who attended more than once.
Those entries cannot establish a waste amount per distinct visitor without further attendance information.
The fair uses a former orchard field and hires its temporary stalls and barriers from several suppliers.
No independently measured emissions reduction or claim of zero waste is supported by the supplied records.
